jomon.description: Hunter-gatherers of the Japanese archipelago, associated with the Jōmon culture, whose DNA forms a deep, distinctive branch of East Asian ancestry. That ancestry is the first of three layers traced in the archipelago, and still a small part of present-day Japanese ancestry.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: What sets the Jōmon-associated individuals apart is how closely they resemble one another. All nine sequenced in a 2021 study share an unusually large amount of genetic drift, the random shifts in gene-variant frequencies that build up fastest in small or isolated populations. They form a tight cluster, apart from other ancient and present-day East and Southeast Asians, which the authors read as a sign of sustained geographic isolation. A second study adds a difference in a single gene: none of the six Jōmon individuals it analysed carries V370A, the East Asian variant of the EDAR gene.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: Three studies supply the genomes, and each covers a different part of the Jōmon record. The 2021 study's nine individuals come from western and central Japan and from four stages of the Jōmon period: Initial, Early, Middle and Late. A second study's seven individuals are dated about 2500–800 BCE. A third study rests on one genome, from an individual known as IK002 who lived on Honshu about 2,500 years ago. It was sequenced at about 1.85-fold coverage, meaning each position in the genome was read fewer than twice on average.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Two studies place Jōmon ancestry on a deep branch of the East Asian family tree. IK002 falls basal to the East and Northeast Asian genomes examined, meaning its lineage split off first, with a strong affinity to Indigenous Taiwanese and the Ainu of Hokkaido. The second study puts Jōmon on a deeply splitting lineage shared with Amur Basin hunter-gatherers and with people of Neolithic and Iron Age Taiwan and of the Tibetan plateau. Its admixture graph, a family tree that allows for mixing, traces just over half of Jōmon ancestry (56%) to a southern lineage related to the ancient Tianyuan genome and the rest to one related to Andaman Islanders.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Later genomes from the archipelago show Jōmon-related ancestry first diluted, then holding steady. Two individuals of the Yayoi culture from northwestern Kyushu fit as roughly half Jōmon and half Northeast Asian-related ancestry, and a model with Jōmon ancestry alone is rejected for them. By the Kofun period an East Asian-related component had joined the mix. Present-day Japanese ancestry is modelled as Kofun-like, with about 15% Jōmon ancestry against about 13% in the Kofun-period individuals.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The evidence is thin partly for a physical reason: Japan's warm, humid climate and acidic volcanic soils, one study notes, generally preserve DNA poorly. The two studies also describe the deep branch differently, one by its place on the family tree, the other as a mix of two lineages, and each picture rests on few genomes. The link to Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherers is partly second-hand: in a PCA, a chart that arranges genomes by overall similarity, IK002 falls between present-day East Asians and ancient Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherers, and the study cites earlier work reporting an affinity between IK002 and an 8,000-year-old Hòabìnhian individual from Laos.

kofun-period-japan.description: The first genomes from Japan's Kofun period, about 1,300 years ago, a time the study describes as a phase of state formation. They carry a third, East Asian-related layer of ancestry on top of the archipelago's earlier Jōmon- and Northeast Asian-related layers.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These three individuals cluster with present-day Japanese in the study's genetic analyses, and they stand apart from the people sampled before them. The comparison is thin on that side too: only two Yayoi-period genomes had been published. A model of Jōmon plus Northeast Asian ancestry, which fits those two Yayoi individuals, is rejected for the Kofun three, so they are genetically distinct from the Yayoi.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The best-fitting model mixes three sources: Jōmon-related, Northeast Asian-related and Han Chinese-related ancestry, the last standing for the East Asian-related layer. The clearest signal is how much the Jōmon share shrank: it is about four times lower than in the sampled Yayoi individuals, which the authors read as an influx of migrants with East Asian ancestry. Simpler two-way models, starting from the Yayoi and adding a Han-, Korean- or Yellow River-related source, give that added source 20–30% of Kofun ancestry, between a fifth and nearly a third.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The three-part structure seen in these individuals has changed little since. Present-day Japanese ancestry is modelled as Kofun-like, with Jōmon ancestry at about 15%, against about 13% in the Kofun individuals. Each figure is uncertain by three to four percentage points either way, so the two are effectively the same, and the authors conclude that the three ancestral components were in place by the Kofun period.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Whether the East Asian-related ancestry arrived in a separate, second wave is not settled. Dating the mixing from the DNA itself points to two episodes: Jōmon with Northeast Asian-related ancestry about 3,450 years ago, give or take more than 800 years, and Jōmon with East Asian-related ancestry about 1,750 years ago. But a model with a single source, a Late Bronze Age or Iron Age population of the Yellow River, also passes some tests, with mixing about 1,840 years ago. And with so few genomes from each period, the Kofun profile may not represent the whole archipelago.

amur-hunter-gatherers.description: Hunter-gatherers of the Amur River basin whose genetic profile held steady from about 7,500 to 1,700 years ago, while the Yellow River and West Liao River profiles changed. Amur-related ancestry shows up later in the West Liao River region and in an individual associated with the Heishui Mohe culture.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Amur group is a genetic cluster: its individuals sit tightly together, and the 2021 study finds those from the Early Neolithic through the Xianbei period consistent with being a clade, a single branch of the family tree. The label “hunter-gatherers” needs care: the 2020 study notes that Amur populations relied on hunting, fishing, animal husbandry and some cultivation into the historic era.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: The 2020 study’s six Amur individuals span the Early Neolithic and the Iron Age: two hunter-gatherers dated about 5525–5320 BCE, and four from the Iron Age, three of them from a Xianbei context. The 2021 study adds 18 individuals at Boisman-2, dated 5400–3600 BCE, and finds the cluster continuing through the Iron Age and the Xianbei period. The 2020 study’s claim of stability across thousands of years rests on those six.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Amur cluster sits on an old branch of East Asian ancestry: the 2021 study finds that Amur Basin hunter-gatherers share a deeply splitting lineage, one that branches off early in the family tree, with Jōmon-associated hunter-gatherers and with Neolithic and Iron Age people of Taiwan and the Tibetan plateau. In a separate model from the same study, Amur hunter-gatherers are about 87% Mongolian Neolithic-related, and the remaining 13% is Jōmon-related.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Amur-related ancestry turns up in later populations in at least two places. In the West Liao River region, farming intensified in the Late Neolithic alongside more Yellow River affinity, and Bronze Age pastoralism coincides with more Amur affinity. An individual associated with the Heishui Mohe culture, from about 1100 CE, is estimated to have 43% Amur Basin Neolithic ancestry, give or take 15 percentage points, with the rest well modelled by a Han Chinese-related source.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: At the level of single people, the West Liao River case rests on one Bronze Age individual from a pastoralist context, who is indistinguishable from ancient Amur individuals. Two others are modelled as deriving 21% of their ancestry, give or take 7 points, from that individual, which the authors speculate reflects a recent migration from an Amur-related gene pool. Stability is also not the same as direct descent: a strict test of continuity rejects the ancient group as direct ancestors of present-day Amur populations, which the authors take to mean gene flow within the Amur gene pool.

yellow-river-farmers.description: Neolithic farmers of the Yellow River basin; in one study’s models, farmer-related ancestry contributes a large share to present-day Han Chinese and some Tibetan groups. Their own profile grew closer to that of present-day southern Chinese and Southeast Asians over time.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Yellow River group is a genetic cluster named for its region, and it spans individuals associated with more than one archaeological culture, among them the Yangshao and the Longshan. Crop cultivation was already the dominant way of getting food there by the Middle Neolithic.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: The 2020 study sampled the Yellow River region at ten sites dated from 3550 to 50 BCE, a span of about three and a half thousand years. The Middle Neolithic part of the record is eight individuals associated with the Yangshao culture, about 3550–3050 BCE, and the Late Neolithic part is burials associated with the Longshan culture, about 2275–1844 BCE. The profile had a wide geographic range: ancient individuals from Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi and the upper Yellow River are modelled as a mixture of Yellow River farmers (about 80%) and Amur hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Yellow River profile did not stay fixed. Longshan individuals of the Late Neolithic are genetically closer to present-day southern Chinese and Southeast Asians than the earlier Yangshao individuals, and the Bronze and Iron Age show no further change. A 2021 study infers that a northern lineage related to the ancient Tianyuan genome contributed about 90% of the ancestry of Upper Yellow River Neolithic farmers.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Yellow River farmer-related ancestry is traced into another ancient population and into present-day groups. In the West Liao River region, a rise in Yellow River affinity in the Late Neolithic coincides with intensified farming. Among present-day groups, the 2021 study estimates that ancestry related to Yellow River farmers of around 3000 BCE accounts for 59–84% of most Han Chinese, the remainder coming from a southern source, and for up to about 84% of some Tibetan groups, whose mixing it dates to about 290 BCE–270 CE.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Why the profile moved closer to southern groups is open: the authors link it to a possible northward spread of rice farming. For Tibetans, a model of Sherpa plus Upper Yellow River Late Neolithic ancestry fits and, the authors say, is compatible with northern-origin scenarios for Sino-Tibetan languages, but other models also marginally fit because the genetic data have limited resolution. The Yangshao side of that comparison is small, just eight individuals.

west-liao-river.description: Individuals from the West Liao River region, where changes in ancestry coincide with changes in how people lived: more Yellow River-related ancestry as farming intensified, more Amur-related ancestry with Bronze Age pastoralism.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The West Liao River group is a geographic grouping, not a single genetic profile: it gathers individuals from several sites and periods because they come from the same region. What makes the region informative is that one place can be followed from the Middle Neolithic into the Bronze Age while both ancestry and ways of living changed.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: The 2020 study’s West Liao River sample comes from four sites dated 3694–350 BCE. Its periods are the Middle Neolithic, with individuals associated with the Hongshan culture, the Late Neolithic, with the Lower Xiajiadian culture, and the Bronze Age, with the Upper Xiajiadian culture. Foxtail and broomcorn millets were cultivated in the region from at least 6000 BCE, and how much people relied on millet changed over time with climate and archaeological culture.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Middle Neolithic groups fall between the Amur and Yellow River clusters, and they differ sharply by place: Hongshan-culture individuals carry about 40% Amur-related ancestry, while an individual from a nearby site carries about 75%, a change within about 600 km once Miaozigou is included. Late Neolithic individuals of the Lower Xiajiadian culture are modelled as 74–88% Yellow River-related, the figure depending on the second source used in the model. Bronze Age individuals of the Upper Xiajiadian culture shift back toward Amur-related ancestry. One Bronze Age individual, from a pastoralist context, is indistinguishable from ancient Amur individuals, and two others are modelled as 21%, give or take 7 points, from that individual, which the authors speculate reflects a recent migration from an Amur-related gene pool.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The authors link the shifts to farming intensifying and then partly giving way to pastoralism, but two things changing together does not by itself show that one caused the other. Each period is represented by few individuals, and the authors say the data are insufficient to test whether differences between places persisted into later periods. A 2021 study models West Liao River farmers with different sources, about 67% Upper Yellow River-related and 33% southern Liangdao-related, and finds this mixture absent from the Mongolian and Amur time series, which its authors say conflicts with a simple spread of West Liao River farmers to those regions.

taiwan-iron-age.description: Individuals from Taiwan sampled across about 2,100 years, whose ancestry combines a mostly southern, farmer-related lineage with a smaller northern one. They share their dominant Y-chromosome and maternal lineages with individuals associated with the Lapita culture in Vanuatu.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The group is defined by place and date, not by a shared identity: it holds 46 individuals from two sites in Taiwan, sequenced in a 2021 study. Their dominant Y-chromosome lineage and four maternal lineages, traced through mitochondrial DNA, are also found in present-day Indigenous Taiwanese.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In the study’s admixture graph, a family tree that allows for mixing, these individuals (the study calls them ancient Taiwan farmers) derive about 75% of their ancestry from a southern lineage, likely related to Yangtze River farmers, and about 25% from a northern lineage related to, but distinct from, Yellow River farmers. The study also finds that people of Neolithic and Iron Age Taiwan share a deeply splitting lineage, one that branches off early in the family tree, with Jōmon-associated and Amur Basin hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The northern part of the ancestry is the puzzle: it does not match Yellow River farmers themselves, so the authors infer a further north-to-south movement. A separate study, read here from its abstract only, reports that northern East Asian ancestry spread across southern East Asia after the Neolithic, and that Neolithic southern East Asian and Taiwan Strait individuals show Austronesian-related connections.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The authors speculate that the additional northern movement was linked to foxtail-millet cultivators. A single 75:25 split describes the whole sample, which comes from just two sites across that long span. Sharing lineages with Lapita individuals shows a relationship, not which way descent runs.

caveats: The page makes no claim about language: “Austronesian-related” is a cited study’s label for a genetic connection.

hoabinhian.description: Ancient hunter-gatherers of mainland Southeast Asia. The abstract of a 2018 study by McColl and colleagues reports that Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherer-related ancestry and East Asian farmer-related ancestry both contributed to Southeast Asian diversity.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Hòabìnhian is a label from archaeology rather than genetics, and the studies apply it to ancient hunter-gatherers of Southeast Asia. Most of what the cited evidence says about them comes from comparisons with other groups, not from a description of their own genomes.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In a PCA, a chart that arranges genomes by overall similarity, a cluster of ancient Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherers sits together with the ancient Tianyuan individual, and a Jōmon-context genome, IK002, falls between that cluster and present-day East Asians. The authors of the IK002 study also cite earlier work reporting a genetic affinity between IK002 and an 8,000-year-old Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherer from Laos, so that link is second-hand.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Early farmers at Man Bac in northern Vietnam mix East Asian ancestry related to southern Chinese farmers with ancestry from deeply diverged eastern Eurasian hunter-gatherers, a mixture of the same two kinds that the McColl study reports for Southeast Asia.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Man Bac study, by Lipson and colleagues, calls the hunter-gatherer side of that mixture deeply diverged eastern Eurasian, while the McColl abstract speaks of Hòabìnhian-related ancestry. The link this page draws between the two is a reading of them together, so whether Man Bac’s hunter-gatherer ancestry is specifically Hòabìnhian-related remains open.

sea-neolithic-farmers.description: Early farmers of northern Vietnam, sampled at Man Bac between 4,100 and 3,600 years ago, whose ancestry mixes a southern Chinese farmer-related source with deeply diverged hunter-gatherer ancestry. The same mixture is modelled for present-day Nicobarese and Mlabri.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The group is eight individuals from Man Bac, part of a 2018 study by Lipson and colleagues of 18 individuals from five sites in Vietnam, Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia, dated 4100 to 1700 years ago. Preservation in tropical environments was poor, so coverage, the number of times each position in a genome is read on average, is low for each individual.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Man Bac farmers carry two ancestries: East Asian ancestry related to southern Chinese farmers, and ancestry from deeply diverged eastern Eurasian hunter-gatherers. In one model, Man Bac, Nicobarese and Mlabri are each about 70% from a Southeast Asian farmer-related source and about 30% from a deeply diverging eastern Eurasian source, and the simplest model that fits has a single mixing event shared by their ancestors. One individual, VN29, stands out with an elevated share of “indigenous” ancestry. In the study’s first analysis, farmers at Ban Chiang in Thailand and Vat Komnou in Cambodia cluster with Man Bac.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: A second 2018 study, by McColl and colleagues, reports in its abstract that Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherer-related ancestry and East Asian farmer-related ancestry both contributed to Southeast Asian diversity, a pairing like the one seen at Man Bac. By the Bronze Age, Nui Nap in Vietnam projects close to present-day Vietnamese, and sites in Vietnam and Myanmar show further influxes, which the authors attribute to substantial additional movements of migrants.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: A single site stands for the whole group. The Lipson study calls the hunter-gatherer side of the mixture deeply diverged eastern Eurasian, while the McColl abstract speaks of Hòabìnhian-related ancestry; the link this page draws between them is a reading of the two together, and whether they are the same ancestry remains open.

yellow-river-farmers: the number of Longshan individuals and the radiocarbon basis for the site dates in the 2020 study.

west-liao-river: dates for the Hongshan, Lower Xiajiadian and Upper Xiajiadian groups (the earlier prose gave Hongshan about 3550–3050 BCE and Upper Xiajiadian about 1050–350 BCE, but no cited evidence statement carries those dates), and the names and locations of the four sites.
taiwan-iron-age: the names, locations and archaeological context of the two Taiwan sites, and how the individuals were dated; which of them are Iron Age (the sample is dated about 1300 BCE–800 CE).

taiwan-iron-age: what Liangdao is and why it stands for the southern lineage (the model labels it Liangdao-related; the summary says likely Yangtze-farmer-related), and which present-day Indigenous Taiwanese groups were compared.

hoabinhian: a source defining the Hòabìnhian (what it is archaeologically, its tools, dates and range) and the full text of McColl et al. 2018 (only the abstract is checked), including how many Hòabìnhian genomes it reports and any proportions of Hòabìnhian-related ancestry in Southeast Asian populations.

hoabinhian: whether the 8,000-year-old Laos individual (cited second-hand) is one of the two individuals on the map, and what the Malaysian individual's age and context are; the checked evidence does not mention Malaysia.

sea-neolithic-farmers: what the study means by “indigenous” ancestry for VN29 (the evidence gives only the word), and whether the authors explain the elevated share; how the Man Bac individuals were dated and what archaeological context (burials, subsistence) the study describes.
sea-neolithic-farmers: the order of dates of Ban Chiang, Vat Komnou and Nui Nap within the 4100–1700 years ago range (the evidence gives only the overall range), so “later” can be checked.

yellow-river-farmers: evidence ev-wang2021-3 and ev-wang2021-ea4 say “Han Chinese” and “Tibetan groups” without saying present-day; the prose adds “present-day” (the Tibetan mixing date of 290 BCE–270 CE implies modern sampled groups). Worth adding to the evidence wording.

yellow-river-farmers: the map shows 47 individuals at 11 sites from five publications (sampled 5302–421 BCE, including Shandong Dawenkou, Dinggong and Chengziya labels), while the cited evidence covers a ten-site, 3550–50 BCE sample from one study; the map membership and the evidence do not line up one to one.

west-liao-river: the map holds 11 individuals at 7 sites from 2 publications, sampled 6400–350 BCE (including three Early Neolithic individuals at Wuqi, Yumin and Zhalainuoer), whereas the cited evidence describes four sites dated 3694–350 BCE; the Early Neolithic individuals have no evidence statement.

west-liao-river: ev-ning2020-ea7 is ambiguous about which site is the 'nearby site' (75% Amur-related) and what 'when Miaozigou is included' refers to; the prose repeats the figures without naming the site.
